question.text: Saksham Skills Pvt Ltd (Section 8 FPE on BSE-SSE, skills training) earns (a) INR 1.2 cr from government-funded skilling of rural youth (covered by exemption notification) and (b) INR 60 lakh from corporate training-consultancy to private firms (fee-for-service). How should the SIA describe the GST treatment in the financial-compliance annexure to the Annual Impact Report?

answer.text: Both streams are GST-exempt because the entity is a Section 8 company
Both streams are taxable at 18% because GST makes no distinction for SSE-listed entities
The government-funded skilling is exempt under specific notification; the corporate consultancy stream is taxable at 18% GST (fee-for-service)
Both streams are taxable at 5% concessional GST for Section 8 FPEs on SSE

explanation.text: The Logic: Under GST law, exemption is activity-based rather than entity-based. Specified social-sector services — notably charitable healthcare and certain education/skilling delivered under notified government programmes — are exempt. Purely fee-for-service engagements with private parties (corporate training, advisory and consultancy) are taxable at the standard services rate of 18%. The right description for Saksham Skills therefore separates the government-funded skilling stream (exempt under the relevant notification) from the corporate consultancy stream (taxable at 18%). The Trap: Section 8 company status is a Companies Act construct and does not by itself confer GST exemption. There is no blanket 18% or 5% rate that attaches to SSE-listed entities as a class; GST eligibility is driven by the nature of the supply, not by the listing platform. Note: The Social Impact Assessors workbook does not, on the cited pages, set out the GST treatment of government-funded skilling versus corporate consultancy, the 18% standard rate on services, or input-tax-credit restriction rules. The framing above reflects general CGST/IGST law and notified GST rate schedules rather than a direct workbook citation.
